scenes.heading: Push Hard, Push Fast
scenes.text: Adult CPR rate is 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Think of the beat of 'Stayin' Alive'. Yes, really.

scenes.heading: Depth Matters
scenes.text: Go at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep, but not past 2.4 inches (6 cm). Lower half of the sternum.

scenes.heading: Let It Recoil
scenes.text: Full chest recoil every push. No leaning! Leaning stops the heart from refilling.

scenes.heading: Ratio and Pauses
scenes.text: Without an advanced airway, 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Keep pauses under 10 seconds. Swap compressors every 2 minutes.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: 100-120, 2 inches, 30:2, swap at 2 minutes. 'Hard, fast, full recoil, few pauses.'

quiz.q: What is the adult compression rate?
quiz.explain: AHA recommends 100 to 120 compressions per minute.

quiz.q: Adult compression depth should be?
quiz.explain: At least 2 in (5 cm) and no more than 2.4 in (6 cm).

scenes.heading: Power On First
scenes.text: Arrive, turn the AED on, and follow the voice prompts. It is literally built to coach you.

scenes.heading: Pads on Bare Chest
scenes.text: Dry the chest, remove medication patches, and place pads firmly on bare skin. Upper right, lower left.

scenes.heading: Everybody Clear
scenes.text: Stop CPR while it analyzes. Nobody touches the patient. Then shout clear and press shock if advised.

scenes.heading: Straight Back to CPR
scenes.text: Resume compressions immediately after the shock. Do not wait to check a pulse. Re-analyze after 2 minutes.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: Power, Pads, Analyze, Clear, Shock, CPR. Say it: 'Please Put Another Charge, Stat, CPR.'

quiz.q: What do you do right after delivering a shock?
quiz.explain: Resume compressions right away and re-analyze after 2 minutes.

quiz.q: Where do adult pads go?
choices: Upper right chest and lower left side
quiz.explain: Place on bare skin, upper right chest and lower left side.

scenes.heading: OPA: Unresponsive Only
scenes.text: Oral airway is for unresponsive patients with no gag reflex. Gagging means it is the wrong tool.

scenes.heading: Measure the OPA
scenes.text: Hold it beside the face. Corner of the mouth to the earlobe, or the angle of the jaw.

scenes.heading: NPA Is Gag-Friendly
scenes.text: Nasal airway works on responsive patients with a gag reflex. Lubricate it with water-soluble jelly.

scenes.heading: Measure the NPA
scenes.text: Tip of the nose to the earlobe. Bevel toward the septum. Use caution with suspected severe facial trauma.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: Oral = Out cold, mouth corner to ear. Nasal = No-gag okay, nose tip to ear.

quiz.q: Which patient can receive an OPA?
quiz.explain: OPAs are only for unresponsive patients without a gag reflex.

quiz.q: How do you size an NPA?
quiz.explain: Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe.

scenes.heading: Scene Safety First
scenes.text: Dead heroes save nobody. Check hazards, use BSI, count patients, and call for more help early.

scenes.heading: General Impression
scenes.text: Sick or not sick? Age, position, color, effort. Decide your priority in seconds.

scenes.heading: AVPU Check
scenes.text: Alert, responds to Verbal, responds to Painful, Unresponsive. It is a fast level of consciousness read.

scenes.heading: Then ABCs
scenes.text: Airway, Breathing, Circulation. Fix life threats as you find them, including major bleeding and pulse quality.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: Scene, Impression, AVPU, ABC, Priority. Treat what kills first, then decide: stay or go?

quiz.q: What does the P in AVPU stand for?
quiz.explain: P means responds to painful stimuli.

quiz.q: What comes first in a call?
quiz.explain: Scene size-up and safety come before patient care.

scenes.heading: Adult Pulse
scenes.text: Normal adult heart rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute. Check rate, rhythm, and quality.

scenes.heading: Adult Breathing
scenes.text: Normal adult respiratory rate is 12 to 20 breaths per minute. Under 12 or over 20 deserves attention.

scenes.heading: Blood Pressure
scenes.text: Around 120/80 is a typical adult reading. Below about 90 systolic in a sick patient is a red flag.

scenes.heading: SpO2 and Skin
scenes.text: SpO2 of 95 percent or higher is typical. Also note skin color, temperature, and moisture.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: 60-100 pulse, 12-20 breathing, 120/80 pressure, 95-plus oxygen. 'Sixty, twelve, one-twenty, ninety-five.'

quiz.q: Normal adult respiratory rate?
quiz.explain: Adults typically breathe 12 to 20 times per minute.

quiz.q: Typical normal SpO2 is?
quiz.explain: A healthy SpO2 is usually 95 percent or above.

scenes.heading: B and E
scenes.text: Balance: sudden loss of balance or dizziness. Eyes: sudden vision loss or double vision.

scenes.heading: Face Droop
scenes.text: Ask them to smile. One side sagging is a classic stroke sign.

scenes.heading: Arm Drift
scenes.text: Eyes closed, arms out. One arm drifting down or weak? Suspect stroke.

scenes.heading: Speech and Time
scenes.text: Slurred or strange speech. Note the last known well time and call it in. Time is brain.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: BE-FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time. Check glucose too, since low sugar can mimic stroke.

quiz.q: What does the T in BE-FAST stand for?
choices: Time to call, note last known well
quiz.explain: T is Time: note last known well and activate EMS and the stroke center.

quiz.q: Which condition can mimic a stroke?
quiz.explain: Low blood sugar can cause stroke-like signs, so check glucose.

scenes.heading: Suspect an MI
scenes.text: Chest pressure, sweating, nausea, arm or jaw pain. Get oxygen only if SpO2 is low, and keep them calm and resting.

scenes.heading: Aspirin Time
scenes.text: If no allergy or active bleeding, give aspirin to chew. Typical adult dose is 160 to 325 mg. Follow local protocol.

scenes.heading: Nitro Assist
scenes.text: Help with the patient's own prescribed nitroglycerin under medical direction. Usually need systolic BP above 100.

scenes.heading: Nitro Red Flags
scenes.text: Hold it with low BP, recent erectile dysfunction meds, or if medical control says no. Reassess vitals after each dose.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: Chew the aspirin, check the pressure, patient's own nitro only. 'Chew, check, own.'

quiz.q: How is aspirin given for suspected MI?
quiz.explain: Chewed aspirin absorbs faster, which is why it is given that way.

quiz.q: Before assisting with nitro, check that?
quiz.explain: Nitro can drop blood pressure, so confirm systolic is above 100 per protocol.

scenes.heading: Know the Signs
scenes.text: Hives, swelling of face or tongue, wheezing, trouble breathing, vomiting, low blood pressure after an exposure.

scenes.heading: Epi Auto-Injector
scenes.text: EMTs can use the epinephrine auto-injector. Typical doses are 0.3 mg for adults and 0.15 mg for small children.

scenes.heading: Where to Inject
scenes.text: Outer middle thigh, through clothing if needed. Hold in place for the time on the device label.

scenes.heading: After the Shot
scenes.text: Give oxygen, keep them supine if hypotensive, monitor airway, and call ALS. Symptoms can return.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: Epi in the Eh-thigh. 'Hives plus hard breathing equals epi, don't delay.'

quiz.q: Where is an epi auto-injector given?
quiz.explain: The lateral mid-thigh is the standard injection site.

quiz.q: Typical adult auto-injector dose?
quiz.explain: Adult auto-injectors deliver 0.3 mg; children's deliver 0.15 mg.

scenes.heading: Spot Hypoglycemia
scenes.text: Confused, sweaty, shaky, pale, or acting drunk in a diabetic patient. Check blood glucose if your protocol allows.

scenes.heading: Oral Glucose Rules
scenes.text: Give oral glucose only if the patient is awake, can swallow, and can protect their own airway.

scenes.heading: When Not To
scenes.text: Unresponsive, seizing, or unable to swallow means no oral glucose. Support the airway and call ALS.

scenes.heading: Reassess
scenes.text: Recheck mental status and glucose. Always transport, since insulin can outlast the sugar you gave.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: Awake and Able to swallow gets glucose. 'If they can't chew, don't do.'

quiz.q: When is oral glucose appropriate?
quiz.explain: Only give it to patients who are alert enough to swallow and protect the airway.

quiz.q: Which sign suggests hypoglycemia?
quiz.explain: Sweaty, shaky, confused patients may have low blood sugar.

scenes.heading: Direct Pressure
scenes.text: Life-threatening bleeding first. Apply firm, direct pressure with a dressing, then a pressure bandage.

scenes.heading: Tourniquet Time
scenes.text: Pressure failing on a limb? Tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound, never on a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops.

scenes.heading: Write the Time
scenes.text: Mark the time applied. Do not loosen it in the field. Expect it to hurt, that is normal.

scenes.heading: Shock Signs
scenes.text: Fast pulse, pale cool clammy skin, anxiety, fast breathing, altered mental status. Low blood pressure comes late.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: Press, Tourniquet, Time it. Treat shock: lay flat, keep warm, oxygen if needed, rapid transport.

quiz.q: Where does a limb tourniquet go?
choices: Over the clothing wrinkle at the foot
quiz.explain: Place it about 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint.

quiz.q: Which is a LATE sign of shock?
quiz.explain: Hypotension appears late, after the body's compensation fails.

scenes.heading: Walkers Are Green
scenes.text: Shout for everyone who can walk to move. Those patients are minor, green. Now assess the rest.

scenes.heading: Check Breathing
scenes.text: Not breathing? Reposition the airway once. Still apneic means black. Breathing after repositioning is red. Over 30 per minute is red.

scenes.heading: Perfusion Check
scenes.text: No radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds means red. Control major bleeding as you go.

scenes.heading: Mental Status
scenes.text: Cannot follow simple commands means red. Otherwise, the patient is yellow, delayed.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: 30, 2, Can do: breaths under 30, refill under 2, can follow commands. Any fail means red.

quiz.q: Respiratory rate that makes a START patient red?
quiz.explain: More than 30 breaths per minute is immediate (red).

quiz.q: What color are walking wounded?
quiz.explain: Patients who can walk are minor, tagged green.

scenes.heading: Crowning? Prep!
scenes.text: Head crowning means delivery is imminent. Gently support the head, check for cord around the neck, then dry and warm the newborn.

scenes.heading: APGAR Score
scenes.text: At 1 and 5 minutes score Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration, 0 to 2 each. Seven to 10 is reassuring.

scenes.heading: Rule of Nines
scenes.text: Adult: head 9, each arm 9, chest 18, back 18, each leg 18, groin 1. Kids have a bigger head, smaller legs.

scenes.heading: SAMPLE and OPQRST
scenes.text: SAMPLE: Signs, Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last oral intake, Events. OPQRST: Onset, Provocation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, Time.

scenes.heading: Memory Hook
scenes.text: APGAR is Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration. Nines: 9, 9, 18, 18, 18, 18, 1.

quiz.q: In an adult, each leg (front and back) is about what percent BSA?
quiz.explain: Each adult leg is 18 percent in the rule of nines.

quiz.q: What does the G in APGAR stand for?
quiz.explain: G is Grimace, the reflex irritability response.
